kernelIdea: Some real numbers are not rational. √2 is one: assuming √2 = p/q in lowest terms forces p and q both even, contradicting lowest terms.

kernels.l1: Some lengths cannot be written as a piece of a whole.
kernels.l2: The slanted line across a square is a real length, but no fraction ever fits it exactly. Grown-ups can prove that no fraction ever will.
kernels.l3: There are numbers that are not fractions at all. The square root of 2 is one: if it were the simplest fraction, both its top and bottom would have to be even, and then it was not the simplest after all.
kernels.l4: No rational number squares to 2. Assuming √2 = p/q in lowest terms forces p and q both even, contradicting lowest terms — so √2 is irrational.
kernels.l5: The irrationality of √2 is proved by contradiction from the lowest-terms assumption, using the lemma that n² even implies n even.
kernels.l6: The square root of 2 is not a fraction; the same argument works for the square root of any prime, and a square root is a fraction exactly when the number under it is a perfect square.
kernels.l7: No fraction squares to 2: assuming lowest terms and using that an even square forces an even root yields a contradiction. The argument generalises to the square root of any prime.
kernels.l8: Irrationality of √2 is the failure of ℚ to be integrally closed in ℝ at that point; the rational root theorem generalises it, and e and π are irrational for genuinely harder reasons.
